title: Compassion Benchmark — Daily Research
description: Daily evidence-linked findings on how institutions recognize, respond to, and reduce suffering — scored across 1,155 entities.

items.title: Aug 18: The Last Briefing Said Nothing Changed. Sixteen Scores Did, Six Crossing Bands.
items.content_text: Compassion Benchmark's last briefing, published August 11, told readers that no scores had changed that cycle. That was accurate at the time. Two days later, a backlog of already-reviewed findings was approved for release, and on August 16 sixteen scores moved on the live rankings. Six crossed from one performance band into another: Cerebras Systems, Microsoft AI, Baxter International and Taipei moved down from their top bands, while Uganda and Guinea-Bissau fell into the Critical band. items.title: Aug 11: The Benchmark Caught Its Own Scanner Making the Same Dating Mistake for a Third Time
items.content_text: Compassion Benchmark's nightly review returned tonight after a ten-day pause. The founder had called for the pause, and this catch-up cycle used a wider two-week lookback window, covering July 29 through August 11. Twenty organizations were checked. Seventeen scores were confirmed unchanged. Two AI companies were flagged for a calibration review, not scored as conduct downgrades, and a separate open finding about OpenAI was updated with new evidence but left at its existing, unapplied reading. items.title: Aug 1: The Benchmark Caught Its Own Scanner Attaching a Year-Old Death Toll to a New Kyiv Strike
items.content_text: Fifteen governments, cities, universities and one company were reviewed overnight. Fourteen scores were confirmed within the benchmark's five-point range. One proposal moved forward: Uganda's score would fall from 20.3 to 11.9 of 100, crossing from the Developing band into Critical, after the United Nations Human Rights Office described a widening crackdown on dissent. The finding is logged for a decision, not yet applied, so Uganda's published score stays at 20.3. The night's biggest story was…

items.title: Jul 27: GEO Group's Score Looked 5.3 Points Better Tonight. It Was a Stored Math Error, Not Improved Conduct.
items.content_text: Twenty governments, cities, and companies were reviewed overnight, the fourth and final night of a four-night catch-up review. All twenty scores held within the benchmark's five-point confirmation range, and no bands changed. The one score that looked different, GEO Group at plus 5.3 points, turned out to be a stored math error, not better conduct. The private prison operator's own numbers add up to 12.5, not its published 6.6, so the gap was flagged for correction, not reported as improvement.…

items.content_text: Twenty governments, cities, and companies were reviewed overnight. Seventeen scores held within the benchmark's five-point confirmation range. Tunis had never been individually assessed. A first real review, done as thousands marched in the capital demanding the president's resignation, found conditions 11.9 points worse than the placeholder score implied. items.title: Jul 21: Israel, Russia, and Sudan Reconfirmed at the Benchmark's Absolute Floor of Zero
items.content_text: Fifteen governments, cities, and companies were reviewed overnight, and not one published score changed. Every result landed inside the benchmark's five-point confirmation range; the largest movement was a 3.4-point dip for Verizon. Three countries held at the benchmark's lowest possible score, zero out of 100. items.title: Jul 20: State Farm Falls Two Bands After California Regulators Find 398 Wildfire-Claim Violations
items.content_text: Eight organizations had their published scores corrected this cycle: six companies, one mining company, and one country. It is the benchmark's largest single-night batch of score changes in more than a month. The most serious change: State Farm dropped two full bands, from Established to Critical. California's insurance regulator found 398 violations of state law in a sample of 220 wildfire-claim files from the 2025 Los Angeles fires. items.title: Jul 18: Ukraine Enters the Ledger as the Acting Party in a Civilian-Harm Event for the First Time
items.content_text: Fifteen countries held their published scores steady tonight, the seventh straight cycle without a single score change. Tonight's most important finding involves Ukraine, not Russia. Ukrainian drones struck two Russian logistics warehouses on July 18, killing nine people. Seven of the dead were civilian night-shift workers at a retail distribution center 500 to 700 kilometers from the front line. President Volodymyr Zelensky publicly acknowledged the strikes. A war-crimes warrant against Taliban leaders, which earlier reporting linked to 'this month,' was actually issued a year ago, in July 2025. items.content_text: Eritrea received its first individual review tonight, after sitting at zero out of 100 for months as an unreviewed placeholder score. The review lands on the same zero, because the United Nations says Eritrea's government is still committing crimes against humanity, including indefinite forced military service that amounts to slavery. items.content_text: A UN Fact-Finding Mission formally found that Rapid Support Forces atrocities in El Fasher, Sudan bear 'distinct markers of genocide' and opened an urgent new inquiry into a similar siege forming around El Obeid. items.title: Jul 13: Tunisia's Proposed Score Cut Is Reaffirmed for a Fourth Day With No New Escalation
items.content_text: Tunisia's proposed score cut, from 34.4 to 23.8 out of 100, was reaffirmed for a fourth straight day. No new escalation emerged beyond the mass sentencing of 21 opposition figures already behind the proposal, so the published score stays at 34.4 while the benchmark's editors review the finding. Iran's own conduct -- political executions at a multi-decade high -- intensifies an already-documented pattern, but Iran's score of 2.5 out of 100 sits so close to zero that even a move to the floor falls…

items.title: Jul 12: Anthropic Holds at 59.1 as a Chinese Regulator's Backdoor Claim Fails the Benchmark's Own Test
items.content_text: Anthropic's published score holds at 59.1 out of 100 after a Chinese government cybersecurity platform alleged that its Claude Code tool contains an undisclosed 'backdoor.' The benchmark checked the claim against its own rule for when such a finding can move a score: it needs either a genuine second hidden-tracking episode or a ruling from a neutral regulator or court. Neither condition was met tonight, so the score stays the same, but the watch on Anthropic is now heightened. Tunisia's proposed…

items.content_text: Tunisia's pending score review was reaffirmed for a second day. New evidence from the United Nations Human Rights Council's closing session on July 8, plus further detail on the 25-year prison sentence and roughly $600 million fine against former Truth and Dignity Commission president Sihem Bensedrine, matches the evidence already behind the proposed score of 23.8 out of 100. items.title: Jul 10: Tunisia's First Individual Review Proposes a Score of 23.8, Down From a Never-Checked 34.4
items.content_text: Tunisia received its first individual assessment on July 10. Its published score of 34.4 out of 100 turned out to be a placeholder that no analyst had actually checked. The new evidence-based score is 23.8 out of 100, a drop of 10.6 points, but Tunisia stays in the same performance band, so this is not a full downgrade. items.title: Jul 9: A UN Inquiry Finds Sudan's Conduct Meets the Legal Test for Genocide; Myanmar's War Passes 100,000 Deaths
items.content_text: A United Nations inquiry concluded on July 9 that mass killings and gang rapes committed by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces (RSF) meet the legal definition of genocide. Sudan already scores 0 of 100, the lowest possible mark, so the finding cannot push the score down further -- but it is the most serious atrocity finding this benchmark has recorded this year. Myanmar's civil war has now passed 100,000 deaths since the 2021 coup, with the military responsible for about 7 in 10 civilian deaths; Myanm…
